title: Nawarla Gabarnmang rock shelter
summary: Nawarla Gabarnmang is a large rock shelter on the Arnhem Plateau in Jawoyn Country, southwest Arnhem Land, Northern Territory. Excavation produced radiocarbon dates back to 45,180±910 cal BP and a charcoal drawing on a fallen slab dated to about 28,000 years ago, the oldest confirmed pictograph in Australia. People also dismantled many of its roof pillars over thousands of years.

uncertainty.note: Start is the earliest excavated radiocarbon date, 45,180±910 cal BP (James Cook University record of David et al. 2011), converted as year = 1950 minus cal BP; the authors writing in Landscape Australia say Aboriginal people started to camp at the site "fifty thousand years ago". End is the present: the shelter and its art remain.

as_recorded.value: Fifty thousand years ago, Aboriginal people started to camp at the site

when.display: Occupied from at least 45,180 cal BP to the present

where.modern_name: Nawarla Gabarnmang (Gabarnmung), Jawoyn Country, Arnhem Land plateau, Northern Territory, Australia
where.historical_name: Nawarla Gabarnmang, Jawoyn Country; no polity at the earliest dates

importance.justification: One of the earliest radiocarbon-dated archaeological sites in Australia, with the oldest confirmed pictograph in the country.

reviewer_note: Coordinates rest on Wikidata alone (Q5515272), which sources them from outside this atlas; another database listing (AMSD) gave a point about 100 km away, so uncertainty is set at 15 km. The Landscape Australia article is co-authored by Margaret Katherine, a senior Elder of the Buyhmi clan and traditional owner, with the excavation team. The 45,180 cal BP figure is the earliest dated stone-artefact association; the article says people began camping about 50,000 years ago.
